name: Naka'ela
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: ANU. ix+168 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No statement for Naka'ela; Naka'ela figures only in comparative tables and the Ulat Inai/Three Rivers subgrouping argument (pp.40-47). Stress rules are stated only for other groups: p.83 'Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu.. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word'; plus stress-conditioned vowel reflexes in Kaibobo, Geser, Buru.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 2022. Language death in Indonesia: a sociocultural pandemic. Linguistik Indonesia 40(2).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing; one sociolinguistic paragraph on Naka'ela (quotes Collins 1982:103; 760 words and paradigms collected in 1978; no speakers today).

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 2021. "Culture is a shadow", language as a shade: Fragments of a dead language, Naka'ela. Wacana 22(1): 152-181. DOI 10.17510/wacana.v22i1.1036
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Sections cover sociohistory, genitive marking, agentive and non-volitional verb inflection; no phonology section, transcriptions carry no stress marks (only one length mark, wa:ti 'root', fn.15 p.159). States the only published Naka'ela data total 30 words and announces an in-progress ~750-entry trilingual vocabulary.

sources.citation: Taguchi, Yushin. 1989. Lexicostatistic survey of the languages indigenous to West Seram. In Wyn D. Laidig (ed.), Maluku (Workpapers in Indonesian Languages and Cultures 6), 15-63. Ambon: Pattimura University and SIL.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 4.3.1.9 Naka'ela: ~five speakers at Taniwel, Western Three River Family membership by cognate percentages; no data, no phonology.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 2019. The Naka'ela language: Studying and appreciating the story of an extinct language. Invited paper, International Seminar on Language, Literature, Culture, and Education, Universitas Haluoleo, Kendari, 15-16 November 2019.
